name: GHC Haskell lightweight threads (skynet 1M-spawn benchmark vs pthread/std::thread)
baseline: pthread_create and std::thread (C/C++ OS threads, 8 kB pthread stacks) running the skynet recursive spawn-and-sum benchmark
workload: skynet microbenchmark: a root unit spawns 10 children, each spawns 10 more, down to 1,000,000 leaves that return their ordinal; sums flow back up; time per spawned unit (GHC thread versus OS thread).
claimed_speedup: Haskell (stack-1.4.0/ghc-8.0.1): 0.05-0.06 us per thread (average over 1,000,000) versus pthread 54-73 us and std::thread 52-73 us per thread (average over 10,000): about 900x-1,460x lower cost per unit (derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: C++ side: gcc-6.3.1, Boost.Build variant=release optimization=speed (pthreads created with 8 kB stacks); Haskell side: stack-1.4.0 / ghc-8.0.1, flags not stated
hardware: dual Intel Xeon E5-2620 v4 2.2 GHz, 16C/32T, 64 GB RAM, Linux x86_64
stars_or_usage: 3.3k stars (github.com/ghc/ghc is a read-only mirror of gitlab.haskell.org/ghc/ghc, which was not opened)
tradeoffs: GHC threads are heap-allocated stack chunks scheduled by the GHC runtime (garbage-collected, optional -threaded and -N). Foreign calls and unsafe FFI interact with the scheduler differently from C.
caveats: The baseline is OS threads (pthread_create, std::thread), not the idiomatic C++ answer for massive concurrency. The same page shows Boost.Fiber (C++ user-space fibers, work stealing, tcmalloc) at 0.05-0.09 us per fiber, which matches or beats Go and Erlang, so this is not a claim that the language beats well-tuned C++. Scale differs: the Go/Haskell/Erlang rows average over 1,000,000 spawned units while the pthread/std::thread rows average over only 10,000 threads because the 1,000,000-thread run exhausted resources (so the ratio compares per-unit cost at different sizes). The numbers come from the Boost.Fiber author's own documentation, ported skynet code for the C++ side (performance/thread/skynet_pthread.cpp: detached pthreads plus a mutex and condition-variable buffered channel) versus the upstream Go source's unbuffered channels; toolchains are from 2017 (go1.8.1, ghc-8.0.1, erts-8.3, gcc-6.3.1). Go/Haskell/Erlang compile flags and runtime options (for example GHC +RTS -N) are not stated on the page. The per-language skynet sources are in https://github.com/atemerev/skynet (MIT, last commit 2023-11-10). Tier B, not A, because the workload sizes differ and the non-C++ flags are unstated; rerunning at an equal unit count would settle it. The repo_url is the GHC compiler mirror because the claim is about the compiler/runtime; the skynet Haskell source is haskell/ in atemerev/skynet. The license file is the Glasgow Haskell Compiler License (BSD-3-Clause text).
found_via: WebSearch: 'lightweight threads comparison goroutines vs pthreads creation time Go faster than C pthreads paper evaluation' surfaced the Boost.Fiber performance page; the Haskell row is on the same page.
why_faster: Implied by the page rather than argued: GHC threads are runtime-scheduled green threads, pthreads are OS threads. No explicit mechanism is given.

name: CBQN (BQN array language) - CRLF-to-LF conversion versus plain C
language: BQN (implementation in C, SIMD kernels generated with Singeli)
baseline: Plain scalar C loop for the same line-ending conversion (crlf_to_lf), compiled with clang 15.0.7 -O3 -march=native
workload: Replace every CRLF with LF in a byte buffer of 100 to 1,000,000 bytes with a CRLF about every 100 characters; BQN one-liner (cr!=) with (0 shifted lf!=) filtered by Replicate versus a scalar C loop; the page also reports selection and compiler benchmarks.
claimed_speedup: Page text: BQN breaks even with C at a little under 200 bytes and reaches 5x C's speed on inputs of a few thousand bytes or more with AVX-512 disabled, over 10x with AVX-512 until cache is the bottleneck. Measured on the page (Tiger Lake i5-1135G7): C 0.555 ns/elt for 10k to 1M bytes; CBQN avx2/bmi2/pclmul build 0.106 (10k), 0.094 (30k), 0.107 (1M) ns/elt, about 5.2-5.9x (derived from page data); native build 0.0526 (10k), 0.0507 (30k), 0.0787 (1M) ns/elt, about 7-10.6x (derived from page data). Also: selection from a small table 0.04 ns per element versus 0.2 ns, and a 35% advantage on a compiler benchmark.
compiler_and_flags: C baseline: clang 15.0.7, 'clang -O3 -march=native lineending.c' (gcc 12.2.1 also discussed: branching code, slightly faster at low density, much slower at high). CBQN built at commit 0d2631a2 with FFI, singeli x86-64 avx2 bmi2 pclmul (and a native build)
hardware: Intel Tiger Lake Core i5-1135G7
why_faster: Array primitives are implemented with hand-written SIMD, lookup tables and blocked multi-pass techniques (Replicate compresses with AVX2/AVX-512 mask operations, adapts to sparse inputs), which compilers do not generate from a scalar branching loop (no SIMD scan, movmask or compress idioms from portable C). The page itself says this is a best case: 'Your BQN programs are unlikely to outperform equivalent C programs' and specialized C is always faster.
tradeoffs: Whole-array style only: per-primitive call overhead, benefits grow with array length (hundreds to thousands of elements) and small element types; poor for sequential, data-dependent loops, cryptography with wrapping integer ops, and C++-style object dispatch. Interpreter, so C interop is through an FFI with copying. Licensing is a per-file mix with timsort (MIT) and Ryu (Apache-2.0/Boost) exceptions.
caveats: First-party measurement by the BQN author on one machine; both programs and the compiler line are on the page so it is reproducible. The C baseline is a simple scalar loop the author took from a Dyalog talk, not hand-vectorized C (a SIMD C version would win; the page says so), the benchmark density of 1/100 is described as not particularly favorable, and the speedup is a best case for BQN primitives. The algorithm is not the same in the strict sense: BQN uses a data-parallel mask and Replicate, C a sequential scan. Page is dated 2023 (gcc 12.2.1, clang 15.0.7) and CBQN has changed since.

name: D (gdc, ldc2) matmul with std.numeric.dotProduct in kostya/benchmarks
baseline: C/gcc 16.1.0 and C/clang 22.1.8 (-O3 -march=native -flto=auto, -std=c23) transposed dot-product matmul of 1500x1500 doubles
workload: Allocate, generate and multiply two 1500x1500 double matrices; the D version transposes b and calls std.numeric.dotProduct per output cell, the C version transposes b and runs one scalar accumulation loop.
claimed_speedup: Matmul time (median over runs, Xeon E-2324G): D/gdc 1.505 s, D/ldc2 1.722 s, D/dmd 1.880 s versus C/gcc 3.034 s and C/clang 3.067 s, about 2.0x and 1.8x faster than gcc C (derived from page data). Rust 3.067 s, Zig 3.071 s, Nim/gcc 3.091 s equal C. BLAS-backed rows (D lubeck 0.042 s, C++ Eigen 0.081 s, Julia with OpenBLAS, Nim Arraymancer) are library comparisons and excluded here.
compiler_and_flags: C: gcc 16.1.0 / clang 22.1.8 '-Wall -Wextra -pedantic -Wcast-align -O3 -march=native -flto=auto -Wa,-mbranches-within-32B-boundaries -std=c23'; D: ldc2 1.41.0 '-O5 -release -boundscheck=off', gdc 14.2.0 '-O3 -frelease -finline -fbounds-check=off', dmd v2.111.0 '-O -release -inline -boundscheck=off'
hardware: Intel(R) Xeon(R) E-2324G, Debian forky/sid Docker image, README updated 2026-07-19
why_faster: Derived by the searcher from the source, not stated by the suite: Phobos std.numeric.dotProduct (std/numeric.d) unrolls 16-wide with two partial sums (sum0, sum1), a different floating-point reduction order; the C loop keeps one strict-FP accumulator and is built without -ffast-math, so the compiler cannot reassociate or vectorize it.
tradeoffs: Gain comes from one standard-library kernel, so a C programmer can match it by writing two or more accumulators or using -ffast-math; D's runtime and GC are not involved in the timed loop.
caveats: This is a library-kernel difference, not a language or compiler advantage: the high-level algorithm is the same (transpose plus dot products) but the D reduction order differs, so results can differ in the last bits (the harness only checks within 0.1). The C row is deliberately plain ('written as the average developer would'), unlike the BLAS rows which dominate the table. CPU model and flags are stated, but gcc 16.1 and clang 22 are newer than the D compilers' LLVM/GCC bases. Time includes allocation and matrix generation.

name: Halide
baseline: Expert hand-tuned C++ (OpenMP + Intel IPP), ARM NEON intrinsics/assembly and CUDA implementations of the same image-processing pipelines used as baselines in the PLDI 2013 paper (local Laplacian filters, bilateral grid, camera pipe, etc.)
workload: Image-processing pipelines written once as an algorithm plus a separate schedule (tiling, fusion, vectorization, parallelism): local Laplacian filters (99 stages) and bilateral grid on quad-core x86, plus camera raw pipe and others on ARM/CUDA, versus the hand-tuned expert code for the same pipelines.
claimed_speedup: Paper abstract (per search-result summary): up to 5x faster than hand-tuned C, intrinsics and CUDA code that experts optimized over weeks or months, with 3-4x fewer lines. Results-table rows (labels matched by inference from a garbled extraction): local Laplacian 262-line C++/OpenMP+IPP vs about 62 algorithm + 7 schedule lines, 2.1x faster (secondary summary: 335 ms vs 158 ms); bilateral grid 5.9x faster, 3x shorter.
hardware: Quad-core x86 desktop, ARM and CUDA GPU platforms (exact CPU models not confirmed; paper PDF could not be opened)
why_faster: Decouples the algorithm from its schedule: the programmer or autoscheduler explores loop tiling, producer-consumer fusion, recomputation vs storage, vectorization and parallelism without rewriting the algorithm, which finds locality/parallelism trade-offs that were too laborious to hand-code in C++.
tradeoffs: Embedded DSL: requires writing a Halide pipeline and a schedule (C++17 API or Python bindings), ahead-of-time or JIT compiled through LLVM; schedule quality depends on the expert or autoscheduler; image/array pipelines only, not general code. LICENSE.txt is MIT with apps/bgu under Apache-2.0.
caveats: Numbers come from the WebSearch result summary of the PLDI 2013 paper (https://people.csail.mit.edu/jrk/halide-pldi13.pdf, host not reachable from this environment, so the PDF was not opened); the summarizer itself said the table text was garbled and matched rows by inference, and the abstract's 'up to 5x' disagrees with the 5.9x table row. Baselines are the paper authors' chosen 2012-13 hand-tuned implementations (not -O3 compiled naive code) on 2012 hardware; compiler flags and CPU models not confirmed. The repository does not carry the baselines or the paper's harness, so the claim is not reproducible from the repo alone (tier B, not A). The 'language' here is a C++-embedded DSL, so Halide pipelines are callable directly from C++.

name: ClangJIT (Clang with JIT extensions for C++ templates)
baseline: Ahead-of-time compiled Eigen benchmark (adapted bench/benchmark.cpp) using runtime-sized dynamic matrices, built with the same Clang at -O3 -march=native -ffast-math
workload: Eigen bench/benchmark.cpp adapted: 40,000,000 repeats of small dense matrix operations; AoT runtime-sized matrices versus JIT-instantiated fixed-size matrices for sizes 3, 7 and 16, JIT compile time excluded from the runtime rows.
claimed_speedup: Runtime, 40M repeats, JIT compile time excluded: size 3 JIT 1.0s vs AoT 8.05s; size 7 JIT 8.34s vs AoT 20s; size 16 JIT 35.3s vs AoT 36.2s (about 8x, 2.4x and 1.03x, derived from page data). Compile time (user): JIT build 3.5s total vs AoT double-only 5.3s and AoT three-float-types-with-dispatch 9.7s.
compiler_and_flags: ClangJIT (Clang fork, -fjit, [[clang::jit]] attribute) with -march=native -ffast-math -O3 as stated in the wiki table header; Clang itself built with GCC 8.2.0
hardware: Xeon E5-2699 (exact variant not stated)
tradeoffs: Needs a custom Clang/LLVM fork (not upstream); the program links the compiler infrastructure and compiles templates at run time (JIT start-up cost, memory, requires source or serialized AST available at run time); restrictions on decltype(auto), explicit specializations and pointer arguments listed on the wiki; the WG21 proposal P1609 for [[jit]] has not been adopted.
caveats: The AoT baseline is Eigen with dynamic (runtime-sized) matrices; the wiki's 'single specialization' column (1.01s, 8.45s, 35.1s) shows an AoT build specialized for one known size matches the JIT run time, so the win is over generic AoT code, not over size-specialized AoT code. Win shrinks to 1.03x at size 16. Wiki is first-party and numbers are single runs (no variance given). The paper (arXiv 1904.08555, SC19 P3HPC workshop) could not be opened (arxiv.org blocked), so only the wiki was checked. Whether the JIT'd code gets exactly the same -O3 level as the AoT code is assumed from the wiki's flag header. Repository last commit is Dec 2019.
found_via: WebSearch: 'Clang-JIT C++ template instantiation at runtime speedup over ahead-of-time compiled code paper github' surfaced arXiv 1904.08555 and P1609; repo wiki then opened on github.com.
why_faster: Runtime values (matrix dimensions) become template arguments instantiated at run time, so the optimizer sees fixed sizes and can unroll and vectorize; only the sizes actually used are compiled (wiki: 'performance benefits of many AoT specializations, sometimes better, at a low compile-time cost').

A C build with -ffast-math (or the same loop order) would likely close most of the gap. The Julia file also uses Threads.@threads, and the thread count used for this row is not stated on the README page. Capped at C for the mismatched optimization level.

Text: 'Here we see the OrdinaryDiffEq.jl algorithms once again far in the lead' (LotkaVolterra_wpd.md); 'The OrdinaryDiffEq.jl algorithms come out as faster in each case than the ODEInterface algorithms' (Pleiades_wpd.md). The compared solvers use different algorithms (Verner/Tsit5 RK vs Adams/BDF/Dormand-Prince), so this is partly an algorithm win; wrapped C/Fortran codes are called through Julia with their own callback overhead into the Julia ODE function, which may penalize the baselines. name: regex (Rust regex crate)
baseline: PCRE2 (interpreter and JIT) and RE2 (C/C++ regex engines); Hyperscan also measured
workload: rebar curated barometer: about 38 regex search benchmarks (literals, alternations, dates, Unicode classes, bounded repeats, dictionaries, ReDoS-style patterns, noseyparker rules) across many engines; corroborated by the LangArena Etc::LogParser task (13 log-grep patterns over generated web-server log lines).
claimed_speedup: rebar README summary of search-time benchmarks (geometric mean of per-benchmark speed ratios to the best engine, lower is better): hyperscan 2.37 (28 benchmarks), rust/regex 1.12.2 3.08 (38), pcre2/jit 10.47 6.00 (34), re2 10.39 (31), pcre2 interpreter 114.75 (33). Compile-time summary goes the other way: pcre2 1.41, pcre2/jit 6.20, rust/regex 11.85, re2 12.28. Intersection computed from the repo's recorded rebar CSVs for 2025-12-19 (derived from repo data, not stated on the page): vs PCRE2 JIT rust/regex is faster in 21 of 34 search benchmarks, geometric mean time ratio 2.13x; vs RE2 faster in 27 of 31, 4.3x; vs PCRE2 interpreter faster in 32 of 33, 44x; vs Hyperscan faster in only 12 of 28 (Hyperscan about 1.45x faster overall). LangArena results 2026-10-05, Etc::LogParser: Rust 0.302 s vs C with PCRE2 JIT 0.485 s (clang) and 0.488 s (gcc), about 1.6x, and vs C++ 0.99 s. Same file, Template::Regex ({{(.*?)}} replacement): Rust 3.699 s vs C PCRE2 JIT 1.173 s, so PCRE2 JIT is about 3.2x faster there.
compiler_and_flags: rebar README gives engine versions (rust/regex 1.12.2, pcre2 10.47, re2 2025-11-05) but no compiler flags. LangArena: rustc 1.99.0 'cargo build --release' (opt-level 3), regex 1.12; C side clang 22.1.8 / gcc 16.0.1 with -O2 -fstack-protector-strong -fno-omit-frame-pointer, system PCRE2 with pcre2_jit_compile.
hardware: rebar README does not state the machine. LangArena results file: AMD Ryzen 7 3800X, 78 GB.
why_faster: rebar analysis: finite-automata engines (lazy DFA, one-pass DFA) with SIMD literal prefilters (memchr, Teddy) avoid backtracking and give DFA-speed matching on most patterns; PCRE2 JIT stays faster where JIT-compiled backtracking is cheap (small anchored patterns, capture-heavy cases).
stars_or_usage: 4.0k stars; the regex engine behind ripgrep and much of the Rust ecosystem
tradeoffs: No backreferences or look-around (linear-time guarantee in exchange). Pattern compilation is slower than PCRE2 and RE2. Unicode tables add binary size. Rust API; C++ needs the rure C binding or FFI.
caveats: The rebar summary geometric means are over different benchmark subsets per engine (28 to 38), so only the intersection numbers are like for like; those were derived by me from the repo's recorded CSVs. rebar is written by the regex crate's author and its README says the analysis is biased towards that crate (BIAS.md). Hyperscan beats it overall and PCRE2 JIT wins roughly a third of the benchmarks. rebar README gives no CPU. The LangArena run is independent but its C side builds with -O2 and hand-written glue, and both implementations differ in surrounding code. Template::Regex shows a 3.2x loss to PCRE2 JIT.
found_via: WebSearch 'Rust crate "faster than glibc" string search OR strstr OR strtod OR memmem benchmark SIMD' surfaced memchr and rebar; then opened rebar README (raw.githubusercontent.com) and its record/curated/2025-12-19 CSVs, and kostya/LangArena results/2026-10-05-kostya-ms7c37.js (https://github.com/kostya/LangArena/blob/master/results/2026-10-05-kostya-ms7c37.js).

name: A*PA2 (astar-pairwise-aligner)
baseline: Edlib (C++) and BiWFA / WFA2-lib (C) exact global aligners
workload: Exact global pairwise alignment (edit distance) of long DNA sequences, e.g. ONT reads of a human genome with 6% to 11% divergence, plus synthetic sequences.
claimed_speedup: Repo README: 'up to 20x speedup over other exact aligners and is competitive with approximate aligners'. Paper abstract as quoted in a WebSearch snippet (WABI 2024, LIPIcs 312, paper page blocked): 19x faster than BiWFA and Edlib on >500 kbp ONT reads at 6% divergence; 5.6x at 11 kbp reads with 11% divergence; 0.81x (slower) on 800 bp reads at 11% divergence; A*PA2-simple is 6x to 8x faster than Edlib for sequences of at least 10 kbp.
why_faster: Per the paper snippet: like Edlib it uses Ukkonen band doubling with Myers bit-packing, adding large blocks, SIMD, a new profile and the A* heuristics from A*PA (a different algorithm, not a language effect).
tradeoffs: Gains only on long, low-divergence inputs; slower than Edlib on short, highly divergent reads. Latest commit message mentions 'latest nightly', so a nightly Rust toolchain may be needed (not confirmed). MPL-2.0 is file-level copyleft. Evaluation harness lives in a separate pa-bench repo.
caveats: Only the 'up to 20x' README sentence was verified on a page I opened; the 19x, 5.6x and 0.81x figures are snippet only from the peer-reviewed paper. CPU and flags not found. Pairwise alignment is on the edge of the string-and-text category.
found_via: WebSearch 'A*PA2 exact global sequence alignment Rust faster than Edlib WFA github astarpa2'; opened the repo page and commits feed.

name: Sassy (SIMD approximate string matching)
baseline: Edlib (C++ Myers bit-vector aligner); parasail (C) and SWOffinder also compared in the paper
workload: Searching short DNA/ASCII patterns (up to about 1000 characters) in long texts allowing k edit errors, synthetic data and a human genome search.
claimed_speedup: Paper abstract as returned in a WebSearch snippet (the bioRxiv page itself is blocked here): 4x to 15x faster than Edlib for patterns up to 1000 bp, text throughput near 2 Gbp/s, over 100x faster than parasail, 100x faster than SWOffinder on CRISPR off-target search. stars_or_usage: 169 stars; published on crates.io, bioconda and PyPI (sassy-rs)
tradeoffs: Needs AVX2 or NEON; supports ASCII, DNA and IUPAC alphabets; best for patterns up to about 1000; C bindings, Python bindings and a CLI exist.
caveats: Numbers come from the paper abstract as quoted in a search snippet (snippet only); the preprint, the Bioinformatics article (doi 10.1093/bioinformatics/btag244, listed on the README) and the eval CSVs were not opened. claimed_speedup: 2018 study, Linux (16-CPU Haswell cloud machine), seconds: numeric row filter tsv-filter 5.48 vs mawk 11.31 vs GNU awk 42.80 (about 2.1x and 7.8x, derived from page data); column selection (4.8 GB) tsv-select 4.79 vs mawk 9.51 vs GNU cut 14.46 (about 3.0x vs cut); summary statistics tsv-summarize 15.78 vs GNU Datamash 48.51 (about 3.1x); regex row filter tsv-filter 8.80 vs mawk 17.74 vs GNU awk 29.02, but xsv (Rust) 7.97 is faster; narrow-line column selection (86M short lines) GNU cut 5.60 beats tsv-select 8.26. A third-party README (hck) on a Ryzen 9 3950X shows tsv-select 1.702 s vs GNU cut 8.30 at 7.541 s (about 4.4x, derived).

why_faster: Author's stated reasons: straightforward D with avoidance of GC allocation, LDC link-time and profile-guided optimisation (2018 gain), TSV-only data model (no CSV escape handling, which the docs call computationally more expensive); the tools are single-threaded, so none of the gain is from parallelism.

tradeoffs: TSV-only (no CSV escapes except csv2tsv); a toolkit of single-purpose tools rather than awk-like scripting; D toolchain needed to build.

GNU cut wins the narrow-line benchmark and xsv wins regex filtering. Repo has no commits since 2021-06-13. The 4.4x figure comes from a competitor's README (hck), where the cut version is 8.30.

name: fastgrep (Rust grep)
baseline: GNU grep 3.12 (C)
workload: Recursive searches over a generated corpus of 200 files x 5,000 lines of Rust-like source (sparse and dense matches, case-insensitive, regex, single 100k-line file) and a scaling test of 50 to 500 files.
claimed_speedup: README benchmark table (warm trigram index, LC_ALL=C): -rn 'fn main' 8.82 ms vs GNU grep 32.99 ms (3.74x); -rc 'use ' 8.55 ms vs 84.75 ms (9.91x); -rni error 37.49 ms vs 82.57 ms (2.20x); -rn 'impl\s+Drop' 45.24 vs 73.43 (1.62x); very sparse SubscriptionManager 5.41 vs 39.35 (7.28x); single file 3.70 vs 5.21 (1.41x); but -rl 'fn main' 7.50 ms vs GNU grep 7.12 ms (0.95x, GNU grep faster). Scaling: 1.48x at 50 files, 2.43x at 200, 3.08x at 500.
compiler_and_flags: fastgrep 0.1.9, Rust 1.99.0 release build, Criterion benchmarks; GNU grep 3.12 installed via Homebrew (build flags unknown).
hardware: Apple M2 Max (12 logical CPUs), 32 GB, macOS 27.0.1
why_faster: README: parallel by default across all CPU threads, lazy trigram index that skips non-matching files on repeat searches, SIMD-accelerated literal search.
tradeoffs: Output order is non-deterministic (multi-threaded); deliberate deviations from GNU grep (binary files, long lines). Index cache stored under the OS cache directory and invalidated by mtime and size. Not every GNU grep flag implemented.
caveats: Very new project, first-party numbers. Gains come mostly from 12-thread parallelism and a warm index versus single-threaded GNU grep, not from a faster per-byte scan; the README itself notes --no-index is often faster when the index cannot skip files. Synthetic corpus, small (about 1M lines) so process start-up matters. GNU grep was run on macOS via Homebrew with LC_ALL=C.

name: jumprope (Rust rope)
baseline: librope (C skip-list rope by the same author)
workload: Replaying real text-editing traces (automerge-paper, rustcode, sveltecomponent, seph-blog1) from crdt-benchmarks against a rope: insert/delete at arbitrary positions.
claimed_speedup: README table, single core of a Ryzen 5800X: automerge-paper librope (C) 16.28 ms vs Jumprope 6.66 ms; rustcode 3.93 vs 1.66 ms; sveltecomponent 1.59 vs 0.59 ms; seph-blog1 10.01 vs 3.81 ms (about 2.4x to 2.7x, derived from page data). name: sd (find and replace CLI)
baseline: GNU sed (C), sed -E and plain sed; version not stated
workload: Replace a quote character on about 1.5 GB of JSON; regex replacement (\w+) -> $1$1 on a 55 MB JSON file; literal and regex replacement line-by-line vs across-lines mode on a 36 MB, 1M-line file.
claimed_speedup: README, hyperfine means: simple replacement on ~1.5 GB JSON: sed -E 2.338 s, sed 2.365 s, sd 0.997 s (~2.35 times faster). The README itself calls the syntax examples cherry-picked. sd uses the Rust regex crate while GNU sed uses glibc regex, so large regex gaps are engine differences; literal replacement in default mode is slower than sed.

name: ipnsort and driftsort (Rust std slice::sort_unstable and slice::sort)
baseline: C++ standard library sorts: std::sort and std::stable_sort of libstdc++ and libc++ (benchmark variants cpp_std_gnu / cpp_std_libcxx in the repo)
workload: Sorting 10k u64 values with a hot cache across seven input patterns (ascending, descending, random, random_d20, random_p5, random_s95, random_z1), stable and unstable sorts, on Zen 3.
claimed_speedup: Qualitative only: the author concludes that 'the current Rust standard library unstable sort implementation outperforms the C++ standard library counterparts'. Per-pattern ratios exist only as plot images (stable-hot-u64-10k.png, unstable-hot-u64-10k.png); no numeric speedup appears in the text.
compiler_and_flags: rustc 1.75.0-nightly (2023-10-03) with --release and lto=thin; C/C++ built through build.rs with opt_level(3) and -std=c++20 (-march=native only for the AVX2/AVX-512 contestants); clang 16.0.6 and gcc 13.2.1. The libstdc++ and libc++ variants are separate cargo features (cpp_std_sys, cpp_std_libcxx).
hardware: AMD Ryzen 9 5900X (Zen 3), Linux 6.5, CPU boost enabled
stars_or_usage: 545 stars; ipnsort and driftsort replaced the sorts in the Rust standard library (rust-lang/rust PR 124032)
tradeoffs: Generic over Ord with arbitrary user comparators; written with a lot of unsafe Rust for code-gen reasons but designed to avoid UB on non-strict-weak orderings and panics (the writeup's Ord and exception safety analysis). Needs Rust; stable sort needs auxiliary memory.
caveats: The author of ipnsort wrote the analysis and says so (bias disclaimer). Results are shown only as plots at 10k u64 on one CPU, with 2023 toolchains; the newer libc++ std::sort (bitsetsort-derived, LLVM 17) is described as 'so far untested'. The writeup says C++ std sorts are 'usually quite old', so the win is algorithmic age rather than a Rust language effect. The set of C++ standard libraries in the plot is inferred from build.rs features and the text ('standard library counterparts'); the plot image was not readable. The ipnsort and driftsort introductions compare only against Rust's previous sorts.
found_via: WebSearch 'driftsort ipnsort Rust sort faster than C++ std::sort benchmark sort-research-rs', then the repo's writeup/sort_safety/text.md Performance section and build.rs
why_faster: Newer algorithms than the introsort-style C++ std implementations: ipnsort (pattern-defeating quicksort lineage with a branchless cyclic Lomuto partition and small-sort networks) and driftsort (adaptive merge sort that falls back to quicksort for low-cardinality input); the author attributes the gap to old C++ implementations, not to the language.

name: Sassy
baseline: Edlib (C++ bit-parallel edit-distance library)
workload: Approximate (semi-global) search of DNA patterns of length 20 to 1000 in texts of length 50 to 128,000 bp with up to k=3 edits, no reverse complement; 91 pattern/text combinations in evals/data/match_frac_0_k_3.csv.

caveats: B rests on the README's citation of the peer-reviewed Bioinformatics paper (not opened); the numbers above are my ratios from the repo's CSV and the CPU is not stated on any page opened. Only the DNA profile without reverse complement was checked (other CSVs exist for other k values). Both tools do different work per match position (Sassy's text-direction tiling), so this is not the same algorithm.
found_via: Search 'Rust SIMD library beats C++ implementation peer-reviewed' led to Ragnar Groot Koerkamp's Rust tools; evals/README.md describes the Sassy vs Edlib eval
why_faster: README: bitpacking and SIMD (AVX2 and NEON) with the main novelty of tiling in the text direction.

name: eBay TSV Utilities (tsv-filter, tsv-select, tsv-summarize, tsv-join, csv2tsv)

Losses: narrow column selection GNU cut 5.60 s beat tsv-select 8.26 s, and xsv (Rust) beat tsv-filter on the regex row filter (7.97 s vs 8.80 s) while mawk took 17.74 s.

Single rows: sherlock-en 29.4 GB/s rust/regex vs 26.3 pcre2/jit, 12.1 re2, 32.0 hyperscan; sherlock-ru 35.6 GB/s vs 32.8, 768.1 MB/s, 4.3 GB/s; but sherlock-casei-en 10.5 GB/s vs 18.8 pcre2/jit and 29.2 hyperscan.

name: bladebench Rust raw TCP server
baseline: the same minimal blocking TCP/HTTP server in C (gcc -O2) and C++ (g++ -O2) from the same repo
workload: Single-threaded blocking accept loop that reads once, writes a fixed 'HTTP/1.1 200 OK' response and closes the connection, load-tested with wrk -t8 -c1000 -d10s over loopback.

Compiler versions, CPU and kernel not stated. The C and C++ servers are functionally identical yet differ by 23% (32,976 vs 40,715), which shows the noise level. Flagged, low-confidence record.
